live_plab_copy.stem:
A 73-year-old woman develops sudden right-sided weakness and expressive dysphasia 90 minutes ago. Symptoms persist on arrival at hospital.

What is the most appropriate immediate approach?

options.A: Give oral aspirin before assessing whether thrombolysis may be appropriate
options.B: Activate the acute stroke pathway urgently
options.D: Assume it is a transient ischaemic attack because symptoms may improve
options.E: Wait 24 hours to see whether symptoms resolve

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Activate the acute stroke pathway urgently
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficit is a medical emergency. Rapid specialist assessment and brain imaging are required to determine appropriate acute treatment. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Antiplatelet treatment must be considered in the context of acute stroke imaging and reperfusion eligibility. C. Outpatient imaging is inappropriate. D. Persistent deficits indicate an acute stroke syndrome. E. Time-sensitive treatment may be lost.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In stroke, time from symptom onset matters.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden focal deficit  ↓  stroke pathway  ↓  urgent imaging  ↓  assess reperfusion eligibility.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, oral aspirin first — antiplatelets are part of stroke care, but they must wait until imaging excludes haemorrhage and thrombolysis eligibility is assessed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Persistent focal deficit within hours of onset: activate the stroke pathway for urgent brain imaging.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 28-year-old man has been continuously convulsing for more than 5 minutes.

What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological approach?

options.A: Give a benzodiazepine per the emergency protocol
options.C: Give an oral dose of levetiracetam
options.E: Give IM haloperidol to control agitation

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Give a benzodiazepine per the emergency protocol
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Convulsive status epilepticus requires immediate emergency treatment. A benzodiazepine is used as first-line pharmacological treatment according to the clinical setting and available route. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Prolonged seizures can cause significant harm; treatment is needed at 5 minutes. C. Oral medication is inappropriate during an active prolonged seizure. D. Levetiracetam is second-line after benzodiazepine treatment. E. Antipsychotics do not terminate status epilepticus.
live_plab_copy.pearl: The first question is often "Has this seizure become status epilepticus?"
live_plab_copy.thinking: Prolonged convulsion  ↓  status epilepticus  ↓  emergency benzodiazepine treatment  ↓  reassess.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, IV levetiracetam before a benzodiazepine — levetiracetam is used in status epilepticus, but only as a second-line drug after benzodiazepine treatment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Convulsive seizure lasting beyond 5 minutes: benzodiazepine first, second-line drug only if it continues.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 76-year-old man with Parkinson's disease reports occasional visual hallucinations. He recognises that they are not real and is not distressed by them. His family is also comfortable with the situation.

What is the most appropriate initial approach?

options.A: Start quetiapine to prevent the hallucinations worsening
options.B: Stop levodopa abruptly to remove the likely cause
options.C: Look for medical or drug triggers; treatment may not be needed
options.E: Start olanzapine as the first-line antipsychotic

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Look for medical or drug triggers; treatment may not be needed
live_plab_copy.why_correct: NICE recommends assessment for medical and medication-related causes. If hallucinations are well tolerated, treatment may not be necessary. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Well-tolerated hallucinations do not automatically require antipsychotic treatment. B. Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medication risks acute akinesia and a neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome. D. Dopamine-blocking antipsychotics such as haloperidol may worsen Parkinsonian symptoms. E. Olanzapine should not be offered for Parkinson's disease psychosis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Medication reduction should involve appropriate Parkinson's expertise.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Parkinson's + hallucinations  ↓  look for triggers  ↓  assess impact  ↓  treat only when clinically necessary.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, starting quetiapine — antipsychotic treatment feels proactive, but well-tolerated hallucinations with retained insight may need no drug at all.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Parkinson's hallucinations: look for medical and drug triggers first; tolerated ones may not need treatment.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 61-year-old woman develops sudden vertigo, severe gait ataxia and new dysarthria.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Prescribe prochlorperazine and review in one week
options.B: Treat as a possible central cause and arrange urgent stroke assessment
options.C: Perform a Dix–Hallpike test and Epley manoeuvre as treatment
options.D: Diagnose vestibular neuritis and start oral prochlorperazine and rehabilitation
options.E: Refer routinely to ENT for audiometry and vestibular testing

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: B. Treat as a possible central cause and arrange urgent stroke assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Acute vertigo accompanied by dysarthria and severe gait disturbance raises concern for a central neurological cause such as posterior circulation stroke. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and TIA.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Symptomatic treatment must not replace assessment. C. Dysarthria and severe ataxia are not features of BPPV. D. Vestibular neuritis does not cause dysarthria; neurological deficits are red flags. E. Routine ENT assessment is inappropriate for an acute neurological presentation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: The presence of neurological deficits changes the urgency completely.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Vertigo + focal neurological features  ↓  central cause until appropriately excluded.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, vestibular neuritis — acute vertigo fits, but dysarthria and severe gait ataxia are central signs suggesting a posterior circulation stroke.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Vertigo with dysarthria or severe ataxia is central until proven otherwise: urgent stroke assessment.

A 74-year-old man suddenly develops facial droop, arm weakness and speech difficulty.

What is the appropriate response?

options.E: Wait for symptoms to resolve completely

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. A routine GP appointment would delay time-critical reperfusion treatment. B. There is no indication for antibiotics in an acute focal neurological deficit. C. Rehabilitation follows diagnosis and acute treatment; it does not replace urgent assessment. E. Waiting for resolution wastes the treatment window, and resolved symptoms would still need urgent TIA assessment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A positive FAST (face, arm, speech) means emergency transfer for urgent brain imaging, because thrombolysis and thrombectomy are only possible within a limited time window.
live_plab_copy.thinking: > Sudden focal neurological deficit  ↓  stroke pathway.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, wait for symptoms to resolve — tempting because this might be a TIA, but waiting wastes the reperfusion window, and resolved symptoms would still need urgent TIA assessment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sudden face, arm or speech deficit: treat as stroke and act immediately, as time is brain.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 69-year-old woman develops sudden unilateral arm weakness that completely resolves after 20 minutes.

What should this be regarded as?

options.A: Possible transient ischaemic attack requiring urgent assessment
options.B: Migraine aura without headache, needing routine review
options.C: Focal seizure with Todd's paresis, needing an outpatient EEG
options.D: Hypoglycaemic episode needing dietary advice and monitoring
options.E: Peripheral nerve compression needing routine nerve studies

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Possible transient ischaemic attack requiring urgent assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sudden focal neurological symptoms that resolve completely within 24 hours should be treated as a suspected TIA. NICE NG128 recommends immediate aspirin 300 mg (unless contraindicated) and specialist assessment within 24 hours because of the high early stroke risk.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Migraine aura is usually positive and spreading; sudden negative motor symptoms should not be attributed to migraine. C. There was no seizure; sudden focal weakness that resolves should be treated as a TIA. D. Hypoglycaemia should be excluded, but it does not explain the episode without evidence and the TIA must be assessed. E. Nerve compression causes gradual symptoms, not sudden transient unilateral weakness.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Resolution of symptoms does not make a transient focal neurological event safe to ignore.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden-onset focal deficit ↓ unilateral arm weakness is a negative symptom ↓ complete resolution within 24 hours ↓ high early stroke risk ↓ possible TIA needing urgent assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, migraine aura without headache — tempting as a transient neurological event, but aura is usually positive and spreading; sudden negative motor loss should be managed as TIA.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A sudden focal deficit that fully resolves is a TIA until proven otherwise: assess urgently.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient develops sudden facial weakness. Examination shows weakness of the lower face but preservation of forehead movement. He also has new arm weakness.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Treat as Bell's palsy with oral prednisolone
options.B: Treat as Ramsay Hunt syndrome with aciclovir
options.C: Arrange a routine outpatient MRI of the brain
options.D: Refer for nerve conduction studies of the arm
options.E: Treat as a possible stroke and arrange urgent assessment

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Treat as a possible stroke and arrange urgent assessment
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Lower facial weakness with forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neuron lesion, and the accompanying arm weakness strongly suggests stroke, so urgent stroke assessment is needed (NICE NG128).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Bell's palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion involving the forehead and does not cause limb weakness. B. Ramsay Hunt syndrome is a lower motor neuron palsy and does not cause arm weakness. C. Routine imaging delays urgent stroke assessment. D. The combination of findings indicates a central cause, not a peripheral nerve problem.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Forehead sparing marks an upper motor neuron facial palsy because the forehead has bilateral cortical supply; with limb weakness, it is stroke until proven otherwise.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Facial weakness with forehead sparing + limb deficit ↓ upper motor neuron lesion ↓ stroke pathway.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, Bell's palsy with prednisolone — tempting because of sudden facial weakness, but Bell's palsy involves the forehead and does not cause arm weakness.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Facial weakness sparing the forehead plus limb weakness: think stroke, not Bell's palsy.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A patient has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that continues for several minutes without stopping.

What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Wait until the seizure has lasted 30 minutes before giving any drug
options.B: Insert a bite block to protect the tongue
options.C: Restrain the limbs to prevent injury
options.D: Give an oral benzodiazepine tablet once it stops
options.E: Treat as status epilepticus and start the emergency pathway

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Treat as status epilepticus and start the emergency pathway
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A generalised convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more should be treated as convulsive status epilepticus, a medical emergency (NICE NG217). Follow the status epilepticus pathway: ABC, oxygen, check glucose and give a first-line benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, IV lorazepam if access is available).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Treatment starts at 5 minutes; waiting risks hypoxic brain injury and makes the seizure harder to terminate. B. Putting an object in the mouth can damage teeth or the airway and obstruct breathing. C. Restraining the limbs can cause injury and does not stop the seizure. D. An ongoing prolonged seizure needs prompt buccal, rectal or IV benzodiazepine, not oral treatment afterwards.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus: give a benzodiazepine (buccal midazolam, rectal diazepam or IV lorazepam) without waiting longer.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Prolonged ongoing seizure  ↓  emergency treatment; don't put anything in the mouth.
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, wait 30 minutes before giving any drug — tempting from older definitions of status epilepticus, but treatment starts at 5 minutes, as prolonged seizures cause harm and become harder to stop.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus: treat now.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 28-year-old has a first witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure and has recovered fully.

What is the appropriate next step?

options.B: Tell the patient no further assessment is necessary
options.D: Start lifelong antiseizure treatment without assessment
options.E: Arrange appropriate assessment for a first seizure

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: E. Arrange appropriate assessment for a first seizure
live_plab_copy.why_correct: After a first suspected seizure, NICE NG217 recommends urgent referral to a specialist first seizure service (ideally seen within 2 weeks) to confirm the diagnosis and identify any cause. The patient should also be given safety advice, including DVLA driving guidance.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Epilepsy is not diagnosed automatically after a single seizure; it requires specialist assessment of recurrence risk and exclusion of other causes. B. A first seizure always needs specialist assessment because there may be a structural, metabolic or cardiac cause and there are safety and driving implications. C. There is no basis for assuming the event was deliberate; this would be inappropriate and unsafe. D. Antiseizure medicines should be started only after specialist assessment, not routinely after a single unassessed seizure.
live_plab_copy.pearl: After a first seizure, refer urgently to a first seizure specialist service and give safety advice, including that the patient should stop driving and inform the DVLA.
live_plab_copy.thinking: First generalised tonic-clonic seizure ↓ full recovery does not exclude a cause ↓ one seizure is not automatically epilepsy ↓ needs specialist review plus safety advice ↓ arrange appropriate first-seizure assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, automatically diagnose epilepsy — tempting after a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure, but epilepsy needs specialist assessment of recurrence risk and exclusion of other causes.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: First seizure: urgent specialist assessment and safety advice, not an automatic diagnosis.

A patient with Parkinson's disease develops new visual hallucinations after a medication change.

What should be considered?

options.A: Medication-related or other medical causes should be assessed
options.B: Parkinson's medication should automatically be doubled
options.C: The patient should automatically receive a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic
options.E: The hallucinations must be unrelated to treatment

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Medication-related or other medical causes should be assessed

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected acute stroke: urgent non-contrast CT head to exclude bleeding before reperfusion.

A 70-year-old develops sudden weakness of the right arm and difficulty speaking. The symptoms completely resolve after 30 minutes.

options.A: Suspected transient ischaemic attack requiring urgent assessment
options.B: No further assessment is required because symptoms resolved

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sudden focal neurological symptoms that resolve completely are a suspected TIA; NICE NG128 recommends aspirin 300 mg (unless contraindicated) and specialist assessment within 24 hours because of high early stroke risk.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Complete resolution does not remove the high early risk of stroke. C. Bell's palsy affects the face and does not cause arm weakness or speech difficulty. D. Epilepsy is not confirmed by a single episode of focal weakness and speech disturbance. E. Migraine should not be assumed in an older patient with sudden weakness and speech disturbance.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A sudden focal deficit that fully resolves is a TIA until proven otherwise. Give aspirin 300 mg unless contraindicated and arrange specialist assessment within 24 hours, because early stroke risk is high.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Older patient ↓ Sudden arm weakness and speech difficulty ↓ Complete resolution after 30 minutes ↓ High early stroke risk ↓ Suspected transient ischaemic attack requiring urgent assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, no further assessment because symptoms resolved — tempting as the patient is now well. Early stroke risk after a TIA is high; resolution is the reason to act urgently, not to relax.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Resolved focal deficit = TIA: aspirin now and specialist review within 24 hours.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Forehead weak = LMN facial palsy; forehead spared = UMN lesion such as stroke.

options.A: Diagnose epilepsy and start antiseizure medication
options.B: Discharge with no follow-up as single seizures are common
options.C: Assess and investigate the seizure and refer to a specialist
options.D: Arrange a routine neurology outpatient appointment in six months
options.E: Start levetiracetam and arrange a routine EEG in primary care

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Assess and investigate the seizure and refer to a specialist
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A first seizure needs medical assessment to exclude provoked causes (e.g. hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance, intracranial pathology), an ECG, and urgent referral to a specialist (ideally seen within 2 weeks), together with safety and driving advice (NICE NG217).
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Epilepsy cannot be diagnosed from a single seizure without specialist assessment, and treatment is not usually started after one seizure. B. A first seizure needs assessment to identify the cause and risk of recurrence, with safety and driving advice. D. NICE advises urgent specialist assessment (ideally within 2 weeks), not routine review. E. Antiseizure medication is not usually started after one seizure without specialist assessment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A first seizure needs assessment for provoked causes such as hypoglycaemia, electrolyte disturbance or intracranial pathology, an ECG, urgent specialist referral, and safety and driving advice.
live_plab_copy.thinking: First-ever generalised seizure ↓ Provoked causes must be excluded ↓ Epilepsy diagnosis needs specialist assessment ↓ Assess, investigate and refer to a specialist
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, levetiracetam with routine EEG — it looks proactive, but antiseizure medication is not usually started after one seizure without specialist assessment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: First seizure: assess for a cause, give safety and driving advice and refer urgently.

A patient is being considered for lumbar puncture but has signs suggesting raised intracranial pressure due to a possible intracranial mass.

What is the appropriate approach?

Absence of papilloedema does not exclude raised intracranial pressure. C. Mannitol does not make lumbar puncture safe in the presence of a possible mass lesion. E. If meningitis is suspected, antibiotics should not be delayed for lumbar puncture.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Lumbar puncture with raised intracranial pressure from a mass risks herniation; get imaging or senior advice first, but never delay antibiotics if meningitis is suspected.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Lumbar puncture considered ↓ Signs of raised intracranial pressure ↓ Possible mass lesion, so herniation risk ↓ Neuroimaging or specialist advice before proceeding
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, proceed if there is no papilloedema — normal fundi feel reassuring, but absence of papilloedema does not exclude raised intracranial pressure.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Suspected raised intracranial pressure: imaging or advice before any lumbar puncture.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Ascending weakness after diarrhoea: think Guillain-Barré and monitor FVC for respiratory failure.

Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, CIDP — it causes symmetrical sensory and motor deficits, but it is immune-mediated, not the characteristic B12 complication.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: B12 deficiency with sensory ataxia: subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

live_plab_copy.stem: During an episode of cataplexy, which feature is typical?

options.A: Sudden loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness
options.D: Complete loss of consciousness with prolonged confusion

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Sudden loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Cataplexy consists of sudden transient muscle weakness or paralysis, usually triggered by strong emotion, while consciousness is maintained.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Generalised tonic-clonic movements suggest a generalised seizure. C. Progressive memory loss is not cataplexy. D. Prolonged confusion after loss of consciousness suggests another neurological event. E. Persistent unilateral weakness suggests a focal neurological disorder.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Cataplexy, a sudden emotion-triggered loss of muscle tone with retained awareness, is highly specific for narcolepsy type 1, alongside excessive daytime sleepiness.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Cataplexy ↓ Triggered by strong emotion such as laughter ↓ Sudden transient loss of muscle tone ↓ Consciousness preserved ↓ Sudden loss of muscle tone with preserved consciousness
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, Loss of consciousness with prolonged confusion — collapse suggests a seizure, but cataplexy preserves awareness and has no post-ictal confusion.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Cataplexy is emotion-triggered loss of tone with full consciousness: think narcolepsy.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient becomes markedly unsteady when standing with their feet together and eyes closed, after being relatively stable with their eyes open. What does a positive Romberg test suggest?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A positive Romberg test indicates impaired proprioceptive input or vestibular function, with vision compensating while the eyes are open.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Aphasia is a language disorder. C. Isolated weakness does not produce the characteristic test finding. D. Facial nerve palsy affects facial movement. E. Lower motor neurone disease is characterised by weakness, wasting and reduced reflexes.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Romberg tests position sense, not cerebellar function: a patient with cerebellar ataxia is unsteady even with eyes open, whereas sensory ataxia worsens markedly when the eyes close.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Stable with eyes open ↓ Unsteady when eyes close ↓ Vision was compensating for lost position sense ↓ Positive Romberg ↓ Impaired proprioception
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, Isolated motor weakness — unsteadiness may suggest weakness, but weakness does not worsen specifically when the eyes are closed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: A positive Romberg points to sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia, not cerebellar disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with longstanding diabetes develops reduced sensation in both feet extending upwards in a symmetrical stocking distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Cauda equina syndrome causes saddle sensory disturbance and bladder or bowel dysfunction. B. Stroke usually causes an acute focal neurological deficit. D. Myasthenia causes fatigable weakness rather than sensory loss. E. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis typically produces focal or multifocal neurological episodes rather than a symmetrical stocking distribution.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Diabetic neuropathy begins distally and ascends in a stocking distribution; loss of protective sensation raises ulcer risk, so regular foot review with monofilament testing matters.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, Cauda equina syndrome — bilateral lower-limb sensory change tempts, but it causes saddle anaesthesia and bladder or bowel dysfunction.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Symmetrical stocking sensory loss in diabetes is peripheral neuropathy; protect the feet.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which nerve root predominantly contributes to knee extension?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Knee extension via the quadriceps is predominantly supplied by the femoral nerve, with major contributions from L3 and L4.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. C5–C6 contributes to upper-limb movements. B. S1–S2 contributes mainly to plantarflexion and other lower-limb functions. C. T1–T2 is associated with upper thoracic and upper-limb innervation. D. L5–S1 is not the principal root contribution to knee extension.
live_plab_copy.pearl: The knee jerk tests L3–L4 via the femoral nerve, while the ankle jerk tests S1. Quadriceps weakness with a reduced knee jerk points to an L3–L4 root or femoral nerve lesion.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Knee extension is the movement tested ↓ Performed by quadriceps femoris ↓ Supplied by the femoral nerve ↓ Main root contribution is L3–L4
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, L5–S1 — the familiar lumbar roots of sciatica questions, but they serve ankle dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, not knee extension.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Knee extension and the knee jerk: L3–L4 via the femoral nerve.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient has difficulty lifting the front of the foot while walking. Which movement is impaired?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Foot drop refers to weakness of ankle dorsiflexion, causing difficulty clearing the foot during walking.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Foot drop involves dorsiflexion rather than isolated toe flexion. C. Hip extension is unrelated to the characteristic gait abnormality. D. Plantarflexion weakness is a different motor deficit. E. Knee flexion is not the defining movement affected.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Foot drop, or weak ankle dorsiflexion, produces a high-stepping gait; common causes include common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular neck and L5 radiculopathy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Cannot lift the front of the foot ↓ Toes catch while walking ↓ Tibialis anterior weakness ↓ Ankle dorsiflexion
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, Ankle plantarflexion — the opposite ankle movement and easily confused; plantarflexion weakness affects push-off, not lifting the forefoot.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Foot drop means weak ankle dorsiflexion: think common peroneal nerve or L5.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which finding is most characteristic of a lower motor neurone lesion?
live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Muscle wasting with reduced reflexes
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Lower motor neurone lesions cause weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations and reduced or absent reflexes.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. An extensor plantar response indicates an upper motor neurone lesion. B. Spasticity is an upper motor neurone sign. C. Increased tone and brisk reflexes are upper motor neurone features. E. Clonus is associated with hyperreflexia and upper motor neurone lesions.
live_plab_copy.pearl: LMN lesions give weakness, wasting, fasciculation, reduced tone and reduced or absent reflexes; UMN lesions give spasticity, brisk reflexes, clonus and extensor plantars.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Lower motor neurone damaged ↓ Muscle loses its nerve supply ↓ Wasting and a broken reflex arc ↓ Muscle wasting with reduced reflexes
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, Increased tone and brisk reflexes — often mixed up, but these are upper motor neurone signs; LMN lesions reduce tone and reflexes.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: LMN: wasting, fasciculation, low tone, reduced reflexes; UMN: the opposite.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome develops increasing difficulty breathing and a weak cough. What complication is the greatest immediate concern?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Guillain–Barré syndrome can progress to respiratory muscle paralysis, making respiratory function an immediate priority.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Thyrotoxicosis does not explain progressive respiratory muscle weakness with a weak cough. B. Asthma causes wheeze and bronchospasm and does not explain progressive weakness with a weak cough. C. Hyperventilation should not be assumed; increasing breathlessness with a weak cough in Guillain–Barré syndrome indicates respiratory muscle weakness. D. Functional dyspnoea should not be assumed in Guillain–Barré syndrome, where breathlessness and a weak cough signal impending respiratory failure.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In Guillain–Barré syndrome, monitor forced vital capacity regularly; oxygen saturation falls late, and a falling FVC or weak cough needs urgent critical care review.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Guillain–Barré syndrome ↓ Ascending weakness can reach respiratory muscles ↓ Increasing breathlessness with a weak cough ↓ Neuromuscular respiratory failure
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, Psychogenic hyperventilation — anxiety is common in acute illness, but a weak cough signals respiratory muscle weakness, and blaming anxiety is dangerous.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Breathlessness in Guillain–Barré: measure FVC and escalate early.

live_plab_copy.stem: A previously well older adult suddenly becomes unable to form new memories, repeatedly asking the same questions, while remaining alert and otherwise neurologically intact. The episode resolves within several hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Transient global amnesia causes sudden temporary anterograde memory impairment with repetitive questioning while other neurological functions are relatively preserved.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Delirium causes broader disturbance of attention and awareness. B. A generalised seizure would usually involve impaired consciousness and other seizure features. D. Subarachnoid haemorrhage typically causes sudden severe headache and may cause neurological deterioration. E. Dementia causes persistent rather than transient cognitive impairment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Transient global amnesia causes sudden anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning but preserved identity and alertness, resolving within 24 hours; recurrence is uncommon.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Older adult, sudden onset ↓ Cannot form new memories, repeats questions ↓ Alert and otherwise neurologically intact ↓ Resolves within hours ↓ Transient global amnesia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, Delirium — acute confusion in an older adult tempts, but delirium impairs attention and awareness, whereas here alertness is preserved and only memory fails.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sudden isolated amnesia with repetitive questions, resolving within a day: transient global amnesia.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of a limb. Neurological examination shows findings that are inconsistent with recognised neuroanatomical patterns, and investigations do not demonstrate a structural lesion. What diagnosis may explain the presentation?

options.A: Acute ischaemic stroke in the internal capsule

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Functional neurological disorder can cause genuine neurological symptoms associated with abnormal nervous-system functioning without an explanatory structural lesion; diagnosis is based on positive clinical features of inconsistency or incongruence.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Stroke produces a neurological deficit corresponding to a vascular territory or recognised syndrome. B. Motor neurone disease causes progressive upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction. C. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis produces deficits corresponding to demyelinating lesions, usually visible on MRI. E. A peripheral mononeuropathy follows a recognised nerve-distribution pattern.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Functional neurological disorder is diagnosed on positive signs such as Hoover sign, not simply by excluding disease; explain the diagnosis clearly, as symptoms are genuine, and consider specialist physiotherapy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden limb weakness ↓ Signs inconsistent with neuroanatomy ↓ No structural lesion on investigation ↓ Genuine symptoms from altered nervous-system function ↓ Functional neurological disorder
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis — tempting because MS signs vary, but its deficits follow anatomy and usually show lesions on MRI.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis based on internal inconsistency.

akt_source.why_wrong: A. Fasciculations are associated with lower motor neuron disorders. B. Hyperreflexia is an upper motor neuron sign. D. Chorea consists of involuntary irregular movements. E. Ataxia reflects impaired coordination.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which symptom commonly occurs in Parkinson disease?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Constipation is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson disease and may occur before prominent motor symptoms.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Haematemesis indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding. B. Polyuria is not a defining non-motor feature of Parkinson disease. C. Haemoptysis suggests respiratory or vascular pathology. D. Jaundice indicates hepatobiliary disease.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Constipation is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson disease and may precede the motor signs by years, alongside reduced sense of smell and REM sleep behaviour disorder.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Parkinson disease ↓ Non-motor features are common and may come early ↓ Autonomic involvement of the gut ↓ Constipation
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, polyuria as the defining symptom — urinary problems do occur in Parkinson disease, but urgency is typical and polyuria is not a defining feature.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Constipation is a common, often early, non-motor feature of Parkinson disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops an upper-limb tremor that becomes worse as their finger approaches a target during a finger-nose test. What type of tremor is this?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: An intention tremor becomes more pronounced during targeted voluntary movement and is characteristic of cerebellar dysfunction.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Physiological tremor is usually low amplitude. C. A resting tremor is most prominent when the limb is at rest. D. A postural tremor occurs while maintaining a position. E. Negative myoclonus causes brief lapses in muscle contraction.
live_plab_copy.pearl: An intention tremor worsens as the finger nears a target and points to cerebellar disease; look for dysmetria, nystagmus and ataxia.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Finger-nose test ↓ Tremor worsens near the target ↓ Goal-directed movement tremor ↓ Intention tremor
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, postural tremor — it appears with the arm held out, but it does not progressively worsen as the finger approaches a target.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Tremor worsening as a target is approached is an intention tremor, typically cerebellar.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops drooping eyelids and double vision that become worse towards the end of the day and improve after rest. What is the most characteristic feature?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Myasthenia gravis causes fluctuating weakness that worsens with repeated use and improves with rest, commonly affecting ocular muscles.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Spasticity is an upper motor neurone sign. B. Sensory loss is not a feature of myasthenia gravis. C. Fasciculations indicate lower motor neurone involvement. E. Resting tremor is associated with Parkinson disease.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Fatigable weakness that worsens through the day and improves with rest is the hallmark of myasthenia gravis, often first seen as ptosis and diplopia.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Ptosis and double vision ↓ Worse towards the end of the day ↓ Improve after rest ↓ Fatigable weakness of myasthenia gravis
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, upper motor neurone spasticity — weakness of several muscles can suggest a central cause, but spasticity does not fluctuate with use and rest.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Ptosis and diplopia worse later in the day point to fatigable weakness of myasthenia.

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymic abnormalities, including thymoma.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Adrenal adenoma is not the characteristic association. B. Phaeochromocytoma is an adrenal catecholamine-producing tumour. C. Renal cell carcinoma has no characteristic association with myasthenia gravis. E. Thyroid disease can coexist with autoimmune conditions but is not the characteristic tumour association.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymic abnormalities including thymoma, so every new diagnosis needs CT of the chest.
live_plab_copy.thinking: New myasthenia gravis ↓ Looking for a thymic abnormality ↓ Thymic tumour association ↓ Thymoma
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, thyroid carcinoma — autoimmune thyroid disease can coexist with myasthenia, which tempts, but the characteristic tumour association is thymoma.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma; image the chest.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with proximal leg weakness also reports dry mouth and erectile dysfunction. Which neurological disorder can cause this combination?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Lambert-Eaton syndrome causes proximal weakness and autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth and erectile dysfunction.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Myasthenia gravis causes fatigable ocular, bulbar and limb weakness without autonomic features such as dry mouth. B. MS can cause diverse neurological deficits but this combination is not characteristic. C. Parkinson disease has different motor and non-motor features. D. Polymyositis causes symmetrical proximal weakness without autonomic features such as dry mouth or erectile dysfunction.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Lambert-Eaton syndrome causes proximal weakness with autonomic features and reduced reflexes, and is classically associated with small cell lung cancer.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Proximal leg weakness ↓ Dry mouth and erectile dysfunction ↓ Neuromuscular junction plus autonomic involvement ↓ Lambert-Eaton syndrome
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, myasthenia gravis — another neuromuscular junction disorder, but it mainly affects ocular and bulbar muscles and lacks autonomic features.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Proximal weakness with dry mouth and autonomic symptoms suggests Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with Guillain–Barré syndrome develops fluctuating blood pressure and heart rate. What complication is responsible?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Guillain–Barré syndrome can cause significant autonomic instability, including fluctuations in blood pressure and heart rate.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Raised intraocular pressure does not cause this presentation. C. Cerebellar dysfunction causes coordination problems. D. Optic neuritis is associated particularly with demyelinating disease such as MS. E. Peripheral vascular disease does not explain acute autonomic instability in GBS.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Guillain–Barré syndrome can cause dangerous autonomic instability with swings in blood pressure and arrhythmias, so patients need close cardiac monitoring.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Guillain–Barré syndrome ↓ Peripheral nerve demyelination includes autonomic fibres ↓ Fluctuating blood pressure and heart rate ↓ Autonomic dysfunction
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, peripheral vascular disease — 'peripheral' links it to GBS in the mind, but it is arterial disease and does not cause acute blood pressure swings.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: GBS can cause autonomic instability; monitor heart rhythm and blood pressure.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness of the right side of the face. The forehead is also weak. Which finding supports a lower motor neurone facial nerve lesion?

options.A: Weakness of the lower face with preserved forehead movement
options.D: Weakness of the forehead and lower face

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Weakness of the forehead and lower face
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A lower motor neurone facial nerve lesion affects the entire ipsilateral side of the face, including the forehead.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Forehead sparing suggests an upper motor neurone lesion. B. Bilateral leg weakness suggests a more extensive neurological disorder. C. Shoulder weakness may involve the accessory nerve. E. Isolated tongue weakness suggests hypoglossal nerve involvement.
live_plab_copy.pearl: A lower motor neurone facial palsy weakens the whole half of the face including the forehead; forehead sparing points to an upper motor neurone lesion such as stroke.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden right facial weakness ↓ Forehead also weak ↓ Whole half of the face affected ↓ LMN facial nerve lesion
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, lower face weakness with preserved forehead — the classic facial weakness picture, but forehead sparing indicates an upper motor neurone lesion.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Forehead involved means LMN facial palsy; forehead spared means UMN lesion.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which symptom commonly accompanies migraine?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sensitivity to light is a common accompanying feature of migraine.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Haematuria suggests urinary tract or renal pathology. C. Haemoptysis indicates bleeding from the respiratory tract. D. Jaundice indicates bilirubin accumulation. E. Urinary retention indicates impaired bladder emptying.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Migraine headache is often accompanied by photophobia, phonophobia and nausea; a sudden, worst-ever headache needs a different work-up.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Migraine ↓ Recurrent headache, often with nausea ↓ Common accompanying sensory sensitivity ↓ Photophobia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, urinary retention — a neurological-sounding symptom, but it suggests spinal cord, pelvic or drug causes, not migraine.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Migraine commonly comes with photophobia, phonophobia and nausea.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient suddenly becomes unable to produce or understand meaningful language. Which neurological deficit is present?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Dysphasia is impairment of language production and/or comprehension.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Dysmetria is inaccurate control of movement, often associated with cerebellar dysfunction. B. Ataxia is impaired coordination. D. Diplopia means double vision. E. Dysarthria is impaired articulation of speech despite preserved language.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Dysphasia is a language disorder affecting comprehension or production; sudden onset suggests a dominant-hemisphere stroke.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden inability to produce or understand language ↓ Problem with language itself ↓ Not articulation ↓ Dysphasia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, dysarthria only — it also affects speech, but in dysarthria language is intact and only articulation is impaired.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Dysphasia is a language problem; dysarthria is an articulation problem.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient understands questions and knows what they want to say but their speech is slurred and poorly articulated. What is the most appropriate term?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Dysarthria is impaired articulation caused by dysfunction of the muscles or neurological pathways involved in speech.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Dysmetria refers to impaired accuracy of movement. C. Dysphasia involves impaired language processing or production. D. Aphasia is a language disorder rather than isolated articulation difficulty. E. Dysphagia means difficulty swallowing.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Dysarthria is slurred, poorly articulated speech with preserved language, so comprehension and word choice are normal.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Understands questions ↓ Knows what to say ↓ Speech slurred ↓ Articulation problem: dysarthria
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, dysphasia — the names sound alike, but dysphasia affects language comprehension or formulation, both of which are preserved here.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Intact language with slurred, poorly articulated speech is dysarthria.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops coughing and choking when attempting to drink water after a stroke. What complication should be suspected?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Post-stroke dysphagia can impair swallowing and increase the risk of aspiration.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Internuclear ophthalmoplegia affects eye movements and causes diplopia, not swallowing problems. B. Dysarthria affects speech articulation; coughing and choking on drinking point to impaired swallowing. C. Trigeminal neuralgia causes paroxysmal facial pain, not swallowing problems. E. Expressive dysphasia affects language production, not swallowing.
live_plab_copy.pearl: After stroke, coughing or choking on drinks signals oropharyngeal dysphagia; patients need swallow screening before oral intake to reduce aspiration risk.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Recent stroke ↓ Coughing and choking on water ↓ Impaired swallowing ↓ Oropharyngeal dysphagia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, flaccid dysarthria — bulbar weakness can affect both speech and swallowing, but dysarthria is a speech disorder and does not explain choking on drinks.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Choking on fluids after stroke means dysphagia; screen swallowing before oral intake.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with atrial fibrillation develops sudden focal neurological weakness. Which mechanism is an important cause of ischaemic stroke in atrial fibrillation?

options.D: Venous thrombosis in the leg alone

live_plab_copy.why_correct: AF promotes thrombus formation in the atria, particularly the left atrial appendage, which can embolise to the cerebral circulation.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke but does not explain embolic stroke from AF. B. Hyperthyroidism can predispose to AF but is not itself the embolic mechanism. C. Peripheral nerve compression does not cause cerebral embolism. D. A leg venous thrombus usually causes venous thromboembolism and does not directly produce an arterial stroke without an appropriate shunt.
live_plab_copy.pearl: In AF, stasis in the left atrial appendage forms thrombus that can embolise to the brain; anticoagulation reduces stroke risk.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Atrial fibrillation ↓ Atrial stasis and left atrial appendage thrombus ↓ Embolus to cerebral circulation ↓ Cardioembolism
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, venous thrombosis in the leg alone — clot is the theme, but a leg DVT goes to the lungs and reaches the brain only with a shunt.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: AF causes stroke by cardioembolism from left atrial thrombus.

options.C: Itchy rash, sneezing and watery eyes

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Dysuria, frequency and suprapubic pain suggest lower urinary tract infection. B. Ankle pain does not suggest raised intracranial pressure. C. These symptoms suggest allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. D. Shoulder pain with restricted abduction suggests a musculoskeletal shoulder problem, not raised intracranial pressure.

live_plab_copy.thinking: Headache ↓ Vomiting ↓ Drowsiness from falling consciousness ↓ Raised intracranial pressure
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, itchy rash, sneezing and watery eyes — a three-symptom cluster like the correct answer, but it describes allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, not raised intracranial pressure.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Headache, vomiting and drowsiness together are red flags for raised intracranial pressure.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with Parkinson disease suddenly finds it difficult to initiate walking, particularly when approaching a doorway. What is this phenomenon called?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Freezing of gait is a recognised manifestation of Parkinson disease in which the patient temporarily feels unable to initiate or continue walking.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Levodopa-induced chorea consists of involuntary irregular movements, not difficulty initiating gait. B. Dysmetria is impaired accuracy of movement. D. Cerebellar ataxia is impaired coordination, typically with a broad-based gait. E. Fasciculations are involuntary muscle twitches.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Freezing of gait, a sudden inability to start or continue walking, is often triggered by doorways or turning in Parkinson disease and increases falls risk.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Parkinson disease ↓ Sudden difficulty starting to walk ↓ Triggered by doorways ↓ Freezing of gait
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, cerebellar ataxia — also a gait disorder, but it gives a broad-based unsteady gait, not sudden episodes of being stuck.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Feet 'stuck' at doorways in Parkinson disease is freezing of gait.

live_plab_copy.stem: A middle-aged adult develops progressive involuntary, irregular, jerky movements with behavioural changes. Which movement disorder is characteristic of Huntington disease?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Huntington disease characteristically causes progressive choreiform involuntary movements alongside cognitive and psychiatric manifestations.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Myoclonus is not the characteristic movement disorder of Huntington disease. B. Fasciculations indicate lower motor neurone involvement. D. A resting tremor is characteristic of Parkinson disease. E. Bradykinesia is a key feature of parkinsonism.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Huntington disease causes progressive chorea with cognitive decline and psychiatric change; ask about family history, though new mutations can occur.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Chorea with behavioural change in a middle-aged adult suggests Huntington disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: Which feature helps distinguish myasthenia gravis from many other causes of ocular weakness?

options.E: Pupils are always fixed and dilated

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Reflexes are generally preserved. B. Pupillary constriction is not characteristic. C. Sensory loss is not a feature of MG. E. Fixed dilated pupils are not typical of myasthenia gravis.

live_plab_copy.thinking: Ocular weakness with ptosis or diplopia ↓ Myasthenia affects skeletal muscle at the junction ↓ Pupil muscles are not affected ↓ Pupils usually spared
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, pupils always fixed and dilated — this feature tempts in ocular weakness, but a fixed dilated pupil suggests a compressive third nerve palsy, not myasthenia.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Myasthenia gravis spares the pupils; a dilated pupil means look elsewhere.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient with motor neurone disease develops progressive difficulty speaking and swallowing. What is this most consistent with?

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, cerebellar stroke — it can cause slurred speech, but it is sudden, and progressive speech and swallowing loss in MND reflects bulbar disease.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Progressive speech and swallowing problems in MND mean bulbar involvement.

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Hallucinations do not explain the gait disturbance. B. Hearing loss does not cause this characteristic pattern. D. Loss of smell does not cause ataxia. E. Facial weakness does not cause sensory ataxia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Sensory ataxia from loss of proprioception worsens when the eyes are closed, giving a positive Romberg test; causes include B12 deficiency and peripheral neuropathy.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, isolated hearing loss — inner ear problems can affect balance, but hearing loss alone does not cause gait that worsens with eyes closed.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Gait much worse with eyes closed means proprioceptive loss.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, polyuria from diabetes insipidus — urinary symptoms are common in Parkinson's, but they reflect bladder dysfunction, not diabetes insipidus.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Constipation is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient experiences an electric-shock sensation travelling down the spine and into the limbs when flexing the neck. What is this called?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Lhermitte sign is an electric-shock-like sensation triggered by neck flexion and can occur with cervical cord pathology, including multiple sclerosis.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Murphy sign is associated with acute cholecystitis. B. Babinski sign assesses corticospinal tract function. C. Romberg sign assesses proprioception and balance. D. Tinel sign is used to elicit nerve irritation, often at the wrist in carpal tunnel syndrome.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Lhermitte sign is an electric-shock sensation down the spine and limbs on neck flexion, suggesting cervical cord disease such as multiple sclerosis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Electric-shock sensation ↓ Travels down the spine into the limbs ↓ Triggered by neck flexion ↓ Cervical cord pathology ↓ Lhermitte sign
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, Tinel sign — it also produces tingling, but by tapping over a peripheral nerve such as the median nerve at the wrist.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Electric shocks down the spine on neck flexion are Lhermitte sign.

live_plab_copy.stem: A patient develops sudden weakness and loss of sensation affecting the right side of the body. Which cerebral hemisphere is most likely responsible?

options.C: Peripheral nerves of the right leg only

live_plab_copy.why_correct: The cerebral hemispheres predominantly control the opposite side of the body, so a left hemispheric lesion can cause right-sided weakness and sensory loss.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. A right hemispheric lesion would typically produce left-sided deficits. B. A spinal lesion would depend on its level and pattern. C. A peripheral nerve lesion would not usually affect an entire side of the body. D. Cerebellar lesions mainly cause coordination problems.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Each cerebral hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, so sudden right-sided weakness and numbness point to a left hemisphere lesion, which may also affect language.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness ↓ Right-sided sensory loss ↓ Motor and sensory pathways cross over ↓ Lesion is on the opposite side ↓ Left hemisphere
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, right hemisphere — candidates may link the deficit to the same side, but motor and sensory pathways cross, so right-sided signs mean a left-sided lesion.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Right-sided weakness and sensory loss point to a left hemisphere lesion.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 54-year-old man develops sudden weakness of the right side of his body and difficulty speaking. Symptoms began 45 minutes ago.

What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.D: Reassure and arrange routine GP review

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficits are a medical emergency requiring immediate stroke assessment.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. There is no evidence of bacterial infection. C. Stroke must be excluded before attributing new focal deficits to migraine. D. Delay risks loss of potentially effective acute treatment. E. Routine imaging is inappropriate for a suspected acute stroke.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Sudden focal neurological deficit is a stroke until proven otherwise; urgent assessment and brain imaging decide eligibility for time-critical thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden right-sided weakness ↓ Speech difficulty ↓ Started 45 minutes ago ↓ Within the window for reperfusion treatment ↓ Arrange urgent stroke assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, treat as migraine without assessment — tempting because migraine can cause focal symptoms, but stroke must be excluded first as treatment is time-critical.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sudden focal deficit = emergency stroke assessment; time is brain.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 61-year-old man develops sudden facial drooping, arm weakness and speech difficulty. His blood glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.

Why is checking blood glucose important in suspected stroke?

options.D: Glucose measurement determines whether the stroke is haemorrhagic
options.E: Glucose measurement diagnoses the location of the stroke

live_plab_copy.why_correct: Hypoglycaemia can produce focal neurological deficits resembling stroke and is an important reversible mimic.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Imaging remains important when indicated. B. Hyperglycaemia does not invariably cause stroke. D. Glucose does not distinguish haemorrhagic from ischaemic stroke. E. Glucose cannot localise a cerebral lesion.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke with focal deficits, so check capillary glucose early in every suspected stroke; it is quick to test and easily reversed.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty ↓ Looks like stroke ↓ Hypoglycaemia can produce similar deficits ↓ Glucose check excludes a reversible mimic ↓ Hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, glucose determines whether the stroke is haemorrhagic — tempting as a reason for early tests, but only brain imaging distinguishes haemorrhage from infarction.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Always check glucose in suspected stroke to exclude hypoglycaemia.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 56-year-old man has progressive weakness of the hands. Examination reveals muscle wasting and fasciculations.

Which type of neurological lesion is most consistent with these findings?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Muscle wasting, fasciculations and weakness are characteristic of lower motor neuron involvement.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. UMN lesions typically cause increased tone and reflexes. C. Occipital lesions primarily affect vision. D. Cerebellar lesions primarily cause coordination problems. E. Basal ganglia disease produces movement disorders.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Wasting and fasciculations mark lower motor neuron involvement; if upper motor neuron signs coexist with no sensory loss, think motor neurone disease.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Progressive hand weakness ↓ Muscle wasting ↓ Fasciculations ↓ Anterior horn cell or peripheral nerve pattern ↓ Lower motor neuron lesion
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, upper motor neuron lesion — weakness is shared, but UMN lesions cause spasticity and hyperreflexia without early wasting or fasciculations.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Wasting plus fasciculations means a lower motor neuron lesion.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 34-year-old woman develops sudden weakness and numbness affecting her right arm and leg. She also has difficulty finding and producing words.

Which feature would most strongly support a cortical cerebral lesion?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Aphasia indicates dysfunction of the language-dominant (usually left) cerebral cortex, which is consistent with right-sided weakness, and is a cortical sign that a subcortical or peripheral lesion would not produce.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Isolated foot drop suggests common peroneal nerve or L5 root pathology. B. Isolated calf wasting suggests a lower motor neuron or peripheral process. D. Peripheral nerve pain does not localise to the cerebral cortex. E. An isolated reduced ankle reflex suggests S1 root or peripheral nerve disease.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Cortical signs such as aphasia, neglect or visual field loss localise a stroke to the cortex and help separate anterior circulation strokes from lacunar strokes, which lack them.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Right arm and leg weakness and numbness ↓ Word-finding and production difficulty ↓ Language sits in the dominant, usually left, cortex ↓ Cortical sign ↓ Aphasia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, loss of ankle reflex only — a specific-sounding neurological sign, but it points to S1 root or peripheral nerve disease, not a cerebral cortical lesion.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Aphasia is a cortical sign localising to the dominant hemisphere.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 61-year-old man develops difficulty speaking after a stroke. He understands what is being said but produces slow, effortful speech with relatively few words.

Which type of aphasia is most likely?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Broca aphasia causes non-fluent, effortful speech with relatively preserved comprehension.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Wernicke aphasia causes fluent but impaired, often nonsensical speech with poor comprehension. B. Dysarthria affects articulation rather than language formulation. C. Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. E. Amnesia concerns memory rather than language production.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Broca aphasia is non-fluent, effortful speech with good comprehension (frontal lobe); Wernicke aphasia is fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension (temporal lobe).
live_plab_copy.thinking: Speech difficulty after stroke ↓ Comprehension preserved ↓ Slow, effortful speech with few words ↓ Expressive, non-fluent aphasia ↓ Broca aphasia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, dysarthria — tempting because speech is slow and laboured, but dysarthria is a disorder of articulation, not of producing language.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Broca is broken speech with intact understanding; Wernicke is fluent nonsense.

live_plab_copy.stem:
A 72-year-old man suddenly develops inability to understand spoken language and produces fluent but nonsensical speech.

Which brain region is most likely affected?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Wernicke's area lies in the dominant temporal region and is involved in language comprehension.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. The cerebellum coordinates movement. C. The occipital lobe primarily processes vision. D. The non-dominant parietal lobe does not produce classic Wernicke aphasia. E. The spinal cord cannot cause cortical aphasia.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Wernicke area lies in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, typically within the middle cerebral artery territory; damage gives fluent speech with poor comprehension.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden onset suggests stroke ↓ Cannot understand spoken language ↓ Fluent but nonsensical speech ↓ Receptive (Wernicke) aphasia ↓ Dominant temporal lobe
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, non-dominant parietal lobe only — a cortical answer, but non-dominant parietal lesions cause neglect and spatial problems, not receptive aphasia.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Fluent nonsense with poor comprehension localises to the dominant temporal lobe.

What is the most appropriate initial action?

options.C: Activate the local acute stroke pathway

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: C. Activate the local acute stroke pathway

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, reassure that it is likely migraine — migraine aura can cause focal symptoms, but sudden focal weakness must be treated as stroke; delay loses the treatment window.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: FAST-positive symptoms: activate the stroke pathway immediately.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Fatigable weakness that improves with rest is characteristic of myasthenia gravis.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Parkinson's causes bradykinesia, rigidity and resting tremor. B. Peripheral arterial disease causes exertional limb pain rather than fatigable muscle weakness. C. MS produces neurological deficits separated in time and space. D. Motor neurone disease causes progressive weakness with UMN/LMN signs.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, multiple sclerosis — common in young women and causes fatigue, but it produces deficits separated in time and space, not fatigable weakness that recovers with rest.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Weakness that worsens with use and recovers with rest is myasthenia gravis.

live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sudden onset of a focal neurological deficit is the hallmark of stroke.

Which vascular territory is most likely involved?
live_plab_copy.correct_answer: A. Right middle cerebral artery territory
live_plab_copy.why_correct: A right hemispheric lesion can produce contralateral weakness, sensory loss and visual field deficit, commonly within the MCA territory.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. A left MCA lesion would usually produce right-sided deficits. C. Basilar artery disease produces a different brainstem pattern. D. The radial artery is a peripheral vessel and cannot produce these neurological deficits. E. An optic nerve lesion would not cause hemiparesis.
live_plab_copy.pearl: MCA strokes cause contralateral weakness and sensory loss, face and arm more than leg, with homonymous hemianopia; a dominant-side lesion adds aphasia, a non-dominant one neglect.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Left-sided weakness and sensory loss ↓ Left visual field loss ↓ Contralateral deficits localise to the right hemisphere ↓ Classic MCA pattern ↓ Right middle cerebral artery territory
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, left MCA territory — tempting because the symptoms are left-sided, but hemispheric lesions cause contralateral deficits, so the lesion is on the right.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Hemispheric stroke signs are contralateral: left-sided deficits mean right MCA.

live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, hypothenar muscles — another intrinsic hand group, but supplied mainly by the ulnar nerve, which does not pass through the carpal tunnel.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Median nerve at the wrist = thenar muscles; ulnar nerve = hypothenar and interossei.

akt_source.why_wrong: B. Triceps is supplied by the radial nerve. C. Deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve. D. Hypothenar muscles are supplied mainly by the ulnar nerve. E. Interossei are mainly supplied by the ulnar nerve.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 35-year-old woman has burning pain and tingling over the outer aspect of her thigh. There is no weakness and the symptoms do not extend below the knee. Which diagnosis is most likely?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Meralgia paraesthetica is compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, causing sensory symptoms over the outer thigh without weakness.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Cauda equina syndrome: Causes multiple neurological deficits and possible bladder/bowel dysfunction. B. Femoral neuropathy: Can cause weakness of knee extension and broader sensory loss. C. Sciatica: Usually follows a lumbosacral nerve-root distribution and may extend below the knee. E. Carpal tunnel syndrome: Affects the hand.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Meralgia paraesthetica is a clinical diagnosis: sensory symptoms over the anterolateral thigh with normal power, reflexes and back examination, usually managed by removing the compression.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Burning and tingling over the outer thigh ↓ No weakness ↓ Stops above the knee, so not a root pattern ↓ Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve ↓ Meralgia paraesthetica
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, sciatica — leg pain with tingling suggests a nerve root, but sciatica usually radiates below the knee in a dermatomal pattern.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Outer-thigh sensory symptoms above the knee with normal power = meralgia paraesthetica.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 69-year-old man develops sudden difficulty speaking and weakness of his right arm. Which feature would most strongly suggest an acute stroke rather than a peripheral nerve lesion?

options.A: Gradual onset of weakness over several months
options.B: Symptoms that occur after exercise and resolve with rest
options.C: Isolated numbness of a single fingertip only
options.D: Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
options.E: Pain and tingling in the hand on moving the wrist

live_plab_copy.correct_answer: D. Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sudden focal neurological dysfunction is a classic presentation of acute stroke and requires urgent assessment.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Gradual progression over months is not typical of an acute stroke. B. Exertional symptoms that resolve with rest do not suggest an acute cerebrovascular event. C. Isolated fingertip numbness is more suggestive of a local peripheral nerve problem. E. Movement-related wrist pain and tingling suggest a local musculoskeletal or nerve problem.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Use FAST in the community and ROSIER in the emergency department to recognise stroke; sudden focal deficits need immediate brain imaging to guide thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Older man ↓ Sudden speech difficulty ↓ Sudden right arm weakness ↓ Central pattern, not a single nerve ↓ Sudden onset of focal neurological deficit
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, isolated fingertip numbness — any new neurological symptom may seem worrying, but a tiny isolated area suggests a local digital nerve problem, not stroke.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sudden focal deficit = stroke until proven otherwise; image immediately.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 19-year-old student develops sudden severe unilateral headache associated with photophobia and vomiting. He reports that he has had identical attacks several times previously. Between attacks he is completely well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Recurrent stereotyped attacks of headache with photophobia and vomiting, with complete recovery between episodes, are typical of migraine.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Meningitis usually causes systemic illness with fever and meningeal features. B. Brain tumours usually produce progressive or persistent symptoms. D. Temporal arteritis predominantly affects older adults. E. Subarachnoid haemorrhage typically causes a sudden thunderclap headache and requires urgent assessment.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Migraine is recurrent and stereotyped, often unilateral with photophobia and vomiting, and fully resolves between attacks; a first or worst-ever thunderclap headache needs subarachnoid haemorrhage excluded.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Young adult ↓ Unilateral headache with photophobia and vomiting ↓ Several identical previous attacks ↓ Completely well between attacks ↓ Migraine
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, subarachnoid haemorrhage — sudden severe headache with vomiting tempts, but identical recurrent attacks with full recovery fit migraine rather than a single thunderclap event.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Recurrent identical headaches with full recovery are migraine; a new thunderclap is SAH until excluded.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 42-year-old woman develops proximal muscle weakness. She finds it difficult to climb stairs and lift objects above her head. Sensation is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Predominantly proximal weakness with preserved sensation is characteristic of a muscle disorder.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. MS can cause weakness but does not characteristically present as isolated symmetrical proximal weakness. B. Peripheral neuropathy commonly causes distal weakness and sensory abnormalities. C. Carpal tunnel syndrome affects the median nerve distribution in the hand. E. Radiculopathy follows a nerve-root distribution and often causes pain or sensory changes.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Proximal symmetrical weakness (stairs, lifting overhead) with normal sensation suggests myopathy; check creatine kinase, thyroid function and drugs such as statins or steroids, and consider inflammatory myositis.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Difficulty climbing stairs ↓ Difficulty lifting above the head ↓ Proximal weakness ↓ Sensation normal ↓ Myopathy
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, peripheral neuropathy — weakness makes a nerve cause tempting, but neuropathy is usually distal with sensory loss, whereas here weakness is proximal with normal sensation.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Proximal weakness with intact sensation points to muscle disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops progressive difficulty walking, urinary urgency and cognitive impairment. MRI shows enlarged ventricles without another clear explanation. What diagnosis should be considered?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: The combination of gait disturbance, urinary dysfunction and cognitive impairment is characteristic of normal-pressure hydrocephalus.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Motor neurone disease (ALS) primarily causes progressive motor weakness. C. Parkinson's disease causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor but not this classic triad. D. Primary progressive multiple sclerosis has a different pattern of neurological deficits. E. Progressive supranuclear palsy causes vertical gaze palsy and early falls, not ventricular enlargement.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus gives the triad of gait disturbance, urinary urgency or incontinence and cognitive decline with enlarged ventricles; it is a potentially reversible cause of dementia.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Progressive gait difficulty ↓ Urinary urgency and cognitive impairment ↓ Enlarged ventricles without another cause ↓ Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: C, Parkinson's disease — gait disturbance tempts, but Parkinson's causes bradykinesia, rigidity and tremor and does not explain the triad with enlarged ventricles.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Gait, urine and cognition plus enlarged ventricles: think normal-pressure hydrocephalus.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 69-year-old man develops sudden difficulty speaking but remains able to understand what is being said to him. Which cortical function is most likely affected?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Difficulty producing language with relatively preserved comprehension suggests expressive language impairment.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: B. Comprehension is preserved, which argues against receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia. C. Visuospatial impairment causes neglect or spatial disorientation rather than difficulty producing speech. D. Memory impairment does not cause expressive language difficulty. E. Hearing impairment does not directly cause loss of language production.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Expressive (Broca's) aphasia gives non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension; it localises to the dominant, usually left, inferior frontal lobe.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden onset suggests a vascular event ↓ Difficulty speaking ↓ Understanding preserved ↓ Expressive aphasia ↓ Language production
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: B, language comprehension — aphasia tempts as a whole, but receptive (Wernicke's) aphasia impairs understanding, which is preserved here.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Understands but cannot speak fluently: expressive (Broca's) aphasia.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 27-year-old woman develops sudden weakness of one side of her body while taking a combined oral contraceptive. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficit is a medical emergency and may represent acute stroke.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Cataract causes gradual visual impairment. B. Cystitis causes urinary symptoms. D. Osteoarthritis does not cause sudden hemiparesis. E. Tension headache does not typically cause sudden focal neurological deficit.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Sudden focal neurology is stroke until proven otherwise, even in young adults; oestrogen-containing contraception adds to thrombotic risk.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden one-sided weakness ↓ Focal neurological deficit ↓ Combined pill adds thrombotic risk ↓ Stroke
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, tension headache — it is common in young adults, but it does not cause sudden hemiparesis.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sudden focal weakness at any age needs urgent stroke assessment.

live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Iron does not treat acute neurological deficit. B. Discharge would risk missing an acute stroke. C. Cataract surgery is unrelated. E. Physiotherapy is not the immediate priority.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Sudden weakness with speech disturbance needs immediate stroke-pathway activation and urgent brain imaging, because thrombolysis and thrombectomy are time-critical.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Sudden unilateral weakness ↓ Speech difficulty ↓ Acute stroke likely and treatment is time-dependent ↓ Activate the acute stroke pathway
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: E, outpatient physiotherapy — rehabilitation matters after stroke, but delaying acute assessment loses the window for reperfusion treatment.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Time is brain: suspected stroke means the acute stroke pathway now.

Lumbar puncture does not identify a vascular cause. E. Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Transient focal deficits with full recovery suggest TIA; start antiplatelet treatment and arrange urgent specialist assessment with brain and carotid imaging.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Brief episodes of one-sided weakness and numbness ↓ Complete recovery each time ↓ Recurrent TIAs carry a high early stroke risk ↓ Urgent brain and vascular assessment
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, EEG — recurrent transient episodes may suggest seizures, but sudden negative symptoms such as weakness and numbness with full recovery point to TIA.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: TIA is a stroke warning: urgent specialist and vascular assessment.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 73-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has increasing difficulty initiating movement and frequent falls. Which symptom is typical of Parkinson's disease?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Bradykinesia is a core motor feature of Parkinson's disease.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Haematemesis indicates upper GI bleeding. C. Polyuria has numerous urinary and metabolic causes. D. Hyperreflexia is not the defining motor feature. E. Sudden monocular blindness suggests an ocular vascular emergency.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Parkinson's disease is defined by bradykinesia plus rest tremor and/or rigidity; postural instability and falls tend to develop later.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Parkinson's disease ↓ Difficulty initiating movement ↓ Slowness and progressive reduction of movement ↓ Bradykinesia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: D, hyperreflexia — it is a motor sign, but it reflects upper motor neuron disease and is not the core feature of Parkinson's disease.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Bradykinesia is essential for a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease.

live_plab_copy.stem: A 42-year-old woman has episodes of involuntary muscle contractions in her neck that produce abnormal sustained postures. What term describes this movement disorder?
live_plab_copy.why_correct: Dystonia causes sustained or intermittent muscle contractions producing abnormal movements or postures.
live_plab_copy.why_wrong: A. Tremor is rhythmic involuntary movement. B. Aphasia is impaired language. C. Ataxia is impaired coordination. E. Paraesthesia is an abnormal sensation.
live_plab_copy.pearl: Dystonia is sustained or intermittent muscle contraction causing twisting movements or abnormal postures; cervical dystonia (torticollis) is the commonest focal form.
live_plab_copy.thinking: Involuntary neck muscle contractions ↓ Abnormal sustained postures ↓ Not rhythmic and not incoordination ↓ Dystonia
live_plab_copy.exam_trap: A, tremor — also an involuntary movement disorder, but tremor is a rhythmic oscillation, not a sustained abnormal posture.
live_plab_copy.takeaway: Sustained involuntary contraction with abnormal posture is dystonia.
